title: Mars’s moon Phobos is spiralling inwards and will one day be torn into a ring

cover.alt: Phobos in colour: a lumpy grey-brown potato-shaped moon covered in craters and fine grooves, with the large Stickney crater at its lower right.
cover.credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / University of Arizona · Public domain

body: Phobos orbits just 6,000 km above the surface of Mars, closer to its planet than any other known moon. It circles faster than Mars rotates, so the tides it raises create drag that pulls it slowly inwards, by **about 2 cm a year**. When it gets down to roughly 2.1 Mars radii, tidal forces should break it apart, an estimated 30 to 50 million years from now. Much of the debris would spread into a ring around Mars that might last from 1 to 100 million years, while some would fall into the Martian atmosphere.

slides.prompt: Phobos goes round Mars faster than Mars spins. What does that look like from the ground?
slides.answer: It rises in the west and sets in the east
slides.detail: And it does so twice each Martian day, since one orbit takes only 7 hours and 39 minutes.

slides.heading: When tides should tear Phobos apart
slides.note: Estimates of the time until breakup range from about 30 to 50 million years

slides.heading: True or false for Phobos?

items.text: It is the closest known moon to its planet
It can cause a total eclipse of the Sun
It can’t be seen from near the Martian poles
It is too porous to be solid rock

slides.explanation: Phobos is too small to cover the whole Sun, and it orbits so low over the equator that it never rises above the horizon beyond 70.4° latitude.

slides.heading: Named for fear
slides.text: The American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Phobos on 18 August 1877. It is named after the Greek god of fear and panic, and measures only about 26 by 23 by 18 km.
